caseStudies.summary: From directly leading a 5-engineer automation team to shaping automation strategy and technical standards, with technical influence across a ~70-engineer Quality organization: frameworks, CI/CD with scheduled execution, and a 2,000+ test regression suite.

paragraphs.text: Across two roles at THIQAH, my work moved from directly leading a 5-engineer automation team to shaping automation strategy, tool and framework selection and technical standards, with technical influence across a Quality organization of ~70 engineers.

As Lead Automation Testing Engineer, I designed and evolved web and mobile automation frameworks, reducing test cycle time by 30% across 10+ projects, and scaled the automated regression suite to 2,000+ tests with 95% functional coverage, running through CI/CD pipelines with scheduled execution.

As Staff Engineer, Quality Control Automation, I led test strategy and planning across multiple projects and shaped technical standards, including mandatory CI/CD pipeline integration and scheduled execution.

items.text: The work spanned multiple THIQAH projects and a Quality organization of ~70 engineers, including seniors, leads and technical leads.
It built on my earlier role as Senior Quality Control Engineer, where I owned test design and performance testing for 15+ government projects.
Testing fed release decisions: test governance covered release-readiness assessment, CI/CD quality gates and stakeholder reporting to support go/no-go decisions.

caseStudies.title: LLM & AI Agent Evaluation
caseStudies.summary: Structured evaluation of customer-service AI across nine quality dimensions, using repeatable test scenarios and human review to support vendor acceptance and production-readiness decisions. Worked examples are synthetic.

sections.title: Executive Summary

paragraphs.text: As AI Product Manager at THIQAH, I designed and executed a structured evaluation of customer-service AI across nine quality dimensions, using repeatable test scenarios and human review to support vendor acceptance and production-readiness decisions.

notes: Three kinds of content are kept apart: what I did (labelled CV); standard evaluation methodology (labelled General methodology), which is not a claim that each practice or tool was used in this work; and synthetic worked examples, written for this page and not results from any customer, vendor or production system.

items.text: I own business requirements and solution design for AI-powered customer service (call center) solutions, working with engineering, data and business teams through delivery.
The evaluation supported two kinds of decision: vendor acceptance and production readiness.
Conversational AI can fail in ways functional testing alone doesn't catch: confident but invented answers, unsafe replies, leaked personal data, or following instructions hidden in user input.

sections.title: My Role and Team Collaboration

items.text: Designed and executed the structured evaluation, combining repeatable test scenarios with human review.
Separately, built and prototyped AI agents and agentic workflows, designed prompt strategies, and validated solution concepts using AI-assisted development tools.

notes: Vendor names, evaluation findings and scores from this work are internal and are not published.

items.label: Scenario design
items.text: Designed repeatable test scenarios for the evaluation.

items.label: Test execution
items.text: Executed the scenarios against the customer-service AI under evaluation.

items.label: Nine quality dimensions
items.text: Evaluated correctness, relevance, task completion, hallucination, safety, prompt-injection resistance, privacy/PII handling, multilingual comprehension and conversational robustness.

items.label: Human review
items.text: Used human review of responses as part of the evaluation.

groups.title: Standard evaluation methodology

items.label: Evaluation datasets
items.text: Keep scenarios in a versioned set recording the input, the expected behaviour and the dimensions each scenario tests, so runs can be compared.

items.label: Scoring rubrics
items.text: Define what pass, partial and fail look like for each dimension, so different reviewers score consistently.

items.label: Regression evaluation
items.text: Re-run the same scenario set after model, prompt or configuration changes and compare results with the previous run.

items.label: Limitations and interpretation
items.text: Read results as evidence about a specific configuration and decision, not as a general quality score.

groups.note: General practice for evaluations like this one. It is not a claim that each step or tool was used in the work described above.

items.label: Correctness
items.text: The answer is factually right and consistent with the approved source information.

items.label: Relevance
items.text: The answer addresses what the customer actually asked, without off-topic content.

items.label: Task completion
items.text: The assistant achieves the customer's goal, or hands off correctly, rather than only replying.

items.label: Hallucination
items.text: The assistant doesn't invent facts, policies, prices or actions that its sources don't support.

items.label: Safety
items.text: Harmful, abusive or out-of-policy requests are refused or redirected appropriately.

items.label: Prompt-injection resistance
items.text: Instructions hidden in user input or retrieved content don't override the assistant's rules.

items.label: Privacy / PII protection
items.text: Personal data isn't disclosed to the wrong person or requested without need.

items.label: Multilingual comprehension
items.text: The assistant understands and answers correctly in the languages customers use, including mixed-language messages.

items.label: Conversational robustness
items.text: The assistant stays coherent across multi-turn conversations, topic changes, corrections, typos and ambiguous messages.

items.label: General trade-off: automated vs human scoring
items.text: Automated or model-based scoring scales to many scenarios but can miss nuance and can itself be wrong; human review catches nuance but takes time and needs consistent rubrics.

sections.title: Results and Evidence

items.text: The evaluation was used to support vendor acceptance and production-readiness decisions.

notes: Vendor names, findings and scores are internal and not published. No results from real systems appear on this page; all worked examples are synthetic.

items.label: Non-determinism
items.text: The same input can produce different outputs, so a single run is weak evidence; repeated runs and regression comparison make results more reliable.

items.label: Scenario coverage
items.text: A scenario set only covers the cases someone thought of. Passing it doesn't prove a failure mode is absent.

items.label: Reviewer judgment
items.text: Human review is partly subjective. Clear rubrics and calibration between reviewers reduce disagreement.

items.label: Configuration-specific results
items.text: Results apply to the model, prompts, knowledge sources and integrations that were tested, and need re-checking after changes.

sections.title: Executive Summary

paragraphs.text: QCVerse is an independent AI-powered Quality Engineering and Test Automation product, built collaboratively by the QCVerse Team. I have been its Founder & Product Owner since May 2026. It is not a THIQAH initiative.

Its public tools take Quality Engineering work from a user story through test-case drafts and requirement coverage to automation scripts and bug reports, with generated output treated as drafts for human review.

notes: This case study keeps four things separate: my contributions, the QCVerse Team's work, product capabilities as described on the public website, and the results of one illustrative demo run.

items.text: QCVerse targets repetitive groundwork in Quality Engineering: writing test cases from requirements, keeping automation in step with those tests, and documenting defects clearly.
It is built for Quality Engineering teams and starts from material they already have: a user story, a test case, a page's HTML or an issue description.
The stated aim is less groundwork and more engineering judgment: AI produces a structured first draft, and engineers decide what to test and what is ready to ship.

notes: The website credits the product to the QCVerse Team. The product capabilities and design choices below are not claimed as my individual work.

groups.title: Product capabilities, as described on the public website

items.label: Requirement
items.text: Requirement Analysis breaks user stories and backlog items into actors, functional and non-functional requirements, acceptance criteria, edge cases, dependencies and assumptions.

items.label: Test design
items.text: AI Test Case Studio generates test-case drafts from user stories and reports which requirement areas they cover, and where gaps remain, before publishing.

items.label: Publishing
items.text: The Test Case Generator can publish generated test cases to Azure DevOps when an account is connected.

items.label: Automation
items.text: Agentic Automation generates Playwright, Robot Framework or Selenium scripts from a user story and its linked test cases, for review, copying or download. It needs an AI provider key and an Azure DevOps or Jira connection.

items.label: Defect reporting
items.text: Smart Bug Creation drafts structured bug reports from a description or screenshots.

items.label: Supporting tools
items.text: The Locator Generator produces scored element locators from a page's HTML using rule-based matching in the browser, with no AI involved. The Prompt Library offers prompt templates for functional and automation testing.
Each step is its own tool, so teams can start wherever they are.

sections.title: Key Decisions

groups.title: Product design choices visible on the public website (shared QCVerse Team decisions)

items.label: Drafts, not final output
items.text: Generated test cases and bug reports are drafts that engineers review and edit before anything is published.

items.label: A narrowly defined coverage figure
items.text: Reported AI requirement coverage shows how drafts map to a requirement. It is not executed test coverage, code coverage or automation coverage, and it is capped at 99% by design because it still needs human review.

items.label: Bring your own AI key
items.text: AI-powered tools use the user's own AI provider key, kept only for the current browser session and cleared on reload or sign-out.

items.label: Rule-based where AI isn't needed
items.text: The Locator Generator is rule-based, runs in the browser and works without an AI key.

items.label: Optional integrations
items.text: Azure DevOps and Jira connections are optional; the tools available depend on account permissions, enabled features and connected services.

items.label: Honest about availability
items.text: When a capability is temporarily unavailable, the product says so plainly.

notes: These are product-level choices visible on the public website. QCVerse decisions are shared across the QCVerse Team, so they are not attributed to me individually.
